title: A cauldron of unholy loves (3.1)
tomorrow: what book could set a bored student's heart on fire?

segments.voice: Yesterday, a gang at a pear tree, and a boy who'd never have done it alone. The line was not alone: company pulls both ways.

First night in a new city. Music through the wall, ads on every bus, a party somewhere down the hall, and everyone around you chasing something. Augustine knew that night. Book three of the Confessions opens with him arriving to study, far from his mother's house. In Pusey's translation: "To Carthage I came." Four plain words. And what was singing in his ears? He tells us. All around him, he says, sang "a cauldron of unholy loves."
screen: `FIRST NIGHT IN A NEW CITY.` → `TO CARTHAGE I CAME.` → `A CAULDRON OF UNHOLY LOVES.`

segments.voice: His Latin word for the cauldron is sartago, a frying pan, and the city is Carthago; some readers hear the city itself sizzling. Notice what's in the pan: loves. Not hatred. Augustine's trouble in Carthage is that he loves badly, too fast, in the wrong directions. Then a line that cuts close. He wasn't in love yet, he says, but he loved to love. He was starving for an inner food, God himself, and didn't feel the hunger. So he went looking for something to love, and found it came with jealousy, suspicion, fear, anger and quarrels, like being beaten with burning iron rods, in his words. A cauldron isn't only a place. It's an atmosphere: what everyone around you is loving, chasing, watching and wanting, all bubbling at once. What Augustine gives a person this week is a way to stand in it. He doesn't blame the city for his choices. He names the heat honestly, and he names his own hunger underneath it. The restless heart from his first page is the same heart in Carthage, still hungry, looking in the wrong pans.
screen: `SARTAGO, CARTHAGO.` · `HE LOVED TO LOVE.` · `HUNGRY, AND DIDN'T FEEL IT.` · `NAME THE HEAT, NOT BLAME IT.` · then, large: `CARTHAGE.`

segments.voice: Make a small plan, in three quiet steps. Name the cauldron you live in: the feed, the mood at work or school, whatever the people around you are chasing. Name the one pull it has on your loves. Then choose one small thing you'll do the next time that heat rises, and hold that plan in mind until the sit ends.
A cauldron of unholy loves. Augustine's picture of Carthage: a city bubbling with loves aimed the wrong way, and a young man who loved to love.

segments.voice: The line to keep: carthage, the heat he named instead of blaming. That's today, done.
